Keeping Each Other Alive with Moisture: Why the Deepest Care May Mean No Longer Needing Rescue
The spring dried up.
The fish were stranded together on land.
They breathed moisture on one another and kept each other's bodies wet with saliva.
Every trace of moisture might prolong a life a little.
This is xiang ru yi mo: keeping one another moist with saliva.
Later, the four-character phrase came to describe relationships that hold fast through hardship.
Two people keep supporting one another when resources are scarce and their path is narrow.
Neither can truly solve the problem, but each gives the other the little they have.
Such a relationship is certainly moving.
But the Zhuangzi's sentence does not end there.
It continues:
Better than moistening one another on land is returning to rivers and lakes and forgetting one another.
Why would so precious a rescue be “less good” than not rescuing each other?
First, because what the fish really need is not saliva.
They need water.
Saliva becomes important after the spring dries because the ordinary conditions of life have disappeared.
It can delay death. It cannot turn dry land into rivers and lakes.
If we praise only how the fish moisten one another, it is easy to stay with the relationship's moving quality and forget why they must rescue each other this way.
Hardship creates a particularly close dependence.
You give me a little moisture, and I give you some.
Neither can leave, because if either stops, the other may die sooner.
The dependence is real and may be full of goodwill.
But it still rests on a bad condition:
There is no water.
The best outcome is not for the fish to become more skillful at sharing saliva.
It is for them to return to somewhere they can swim.
This does not belittle their mutual care.
When the spring has already dried, telling the fish:
“Truly free relationships should not be dependent. You should each find your own rivers and lakes.”
Only puts an elegant principle ahead of an actual need.
If moistening one another is all they can do now, that little help may determine who survives long enough for water to arrive.
The real question is not:
Is mutual aid better, or independence?
It is:
Have we mistaken the rescue necessary in a crisis for the ideal shape of a relationship, the one most worth preserving forever?
Some people become indispensable through helping others.
The person they help comes back with every difficulty.
Important decisions need the helper's analysis.
When emotions fall apart, they need the helper to steady them.
Whenever life goes wrong, they immediately fill the gap.
Such a relationship can begin in genuine goodwill.
The helper really does solve many problems.
Over time, however, “They need me” becomes the relationship's most stable proof:
As long as they still need me, I know I matter.
The aim of helping may quietly change.
It no longer means only getting the other person through difficulty.
It also means preserving one's own place as rescuer.
When the other person begins judging independently, finding other support, or simply returning less often, the helper feels a loss instead.
As though swimming away when the water returns were a betrayal of the saliva.
The recipient can be caught in the same structure.
Gratitude may lead them to believe:
Since this person saved me at my hardest moment, I must never refuse their advice, choose a path they disapprove of, or let the relationship stop needing them.
Past rescue gradually becomes the right to decide the future.
Truly precious help is rewritten as a debt that can never be repaid.
But moistening each other when the spring is dry does not entitle another fish to decide where you swim once water comes.
Gratitude can be real.
Memory need not be erased.
But what makes help precious cannot be its permanent claim to the center of the recipient's life.
“Forgetting one another in rivers and lakes” is also easily misunderstood.
It does not demand ingratitude.
Nor does it say mature people should need no one.
Fish in rivers and lakes still live in the same waters. They may still meet, travel together, compete, and affect one another.
“Forgetting” is closer to saying:
They need not affirm one another at every moment through a relationship of rescue.
When there is enough water, one fish can swim in its own direction, and the other can do the same. They need not make “who saved whom” the center of their entire lives.
The relationship is no longer sustained by crisis.
Nor does the other appear only as “my savior” or “someone I must save.”
This need not make the relationship shallower.
It may mean the relationship finally need not prove itself real by making both parties unable to leave.
Of course, not all care can end in “no longer being needed.”
Some dependence lasts.
Some people will always need assistance with certain things.
Shared life itself involves interdependence. No one is truly independent of everyone else.
If “eventually needing nobody” becomes the standard of maturity, we use imaginary rivers and lakes to belittle continuing care in the real world.
This essay cannot therefore turn the Zhuangzi's metaphor into a universal plan for life.
What we can retain is a narrower direction:
Where unnecessary dependence can be reduced, do not preserve it merely to sustain a relationship.
Where conditions can be improved, do not ask only for continued individual sacrifice.
Where long-term care is necessary, preserve as far as possible the recipient's own areas of decision, rather than fixing the whole person in the role of recipient because they need help.
The best help may not always allow the helper to leave.
But it does not treat “never being able to leave” as success.
There is another easily missed cost in the fish's mutual care.
Each consumes its own last reserves of moisture.
They sustain each other, and may also exhaust themselves together.
If someone stands beside them praising the greatness of their devotion without looking for water, the praise becomes cruel.
Communities readily celebrate those who fill gaps for one another under bad conditions.
Someone always takes on extra work for colleagues, and their reliability is praised.
Family members keep using private time to cover gaps in care, and the sacrifice is called love.
When resources are scarce, mutual support keeps the system running, and changing the conditions loses its urgency.
Keeping one another alive is a real virtue.
But virtue can also conceal the question:
Why has the water still not returned?
This does not mean every problem can be solved by changing the environment.
Some losses cannot be reversed.
Some crises can only be borne together within limited conditions.
Rivers and lakes may not be waiting somewhere after all.
When better conditions cannot be obtained, demanding only independence may deprive people of the real support they have now.
So “looking for water” and “continuing to share saliva” need not be an either-or choice.
If rescue is needed now, give it.
And keep asking:
Can this rescue be made something that need not continue forever?
Can other resources be added?
Can more people share the burden?
Can the person receiving care gradually recover some abilities?
Can the caregiver also have rest and a life of their own?
If a relationship can continue only through one party's constant depletion, further praise of their feelings does not answer the problem.
Once back in rivers and lakes, will the fish really forget one another?
The story does not say.
Nor does it matter.
Its concern is not whether memory disappears, but whether the conditions of the relationship change.
On land, the other is the sole source of moisture keeping me alive.
In rivers and lakes, water surrounds every fish again.
They can still matter to each other without being each other's sole condition of survival.
A relationship changes meaning when it moves from “Without you I cannot go on” to “I can go on, and still want to meet you.”
The first may be profoundly deep.
The second gives both more freedom, and the relationship more room for genuine choice.
Their mutual care deserves praise.
When the spring dries, turning away from another does not become noble merely because one yearns for rivers and lakes.
But detached from the second half of the sentence, the phrase can turn an ethic for crisis into the highest form of relationship.
As though deeper love meant becoming each other's only support.
As though the more successful the help, the less the recipient should be able to leave.
As though a relationship no longer founded on need meant affection had disappeared.
By placing rivers and lakes afterward, the Zhuangzi interrupts that picture.
Sometimes the deepest care is not keeping the other forever dependent on one's saliva.
It means being willing to look for water.
And when the water returns, not demanding that the other remain on land and keep needing us to prove our earlier help was valuable.
The fish rescue each other on land because they still want to live.
If rivers and lakes reappear one day, fidelity to that rescue does not mean remaining beside the dried-up spring.
It means letting each other become fish that can swim again.
They can remember.
They can meet.
They can even help each other through new difficulties.
They simply no longer need to make hardship the home of their relationship.
Mutual care in hardship is precious.
But where possible, the best care does not prolong that scene forever.
It lets a day come when neither needs the last moisture from another's mouth in order to go on being themselves.

*Textual basis: the passage in the Zhuangzi, “The Great Ancestral Teacher”: “When the spring dries, the fish are stranded together on land, breathing moisture on one another and moistening one another with saliva; better to forget one another in rivers and lakes.” This essay addresses only the metaphor's local questions of mutual aid in hardship, dependence, and changed conditions. It does not equate them with a complete interpretation of the chapter's treatment of life, death, transformation, and the Dao, nor modernize “forgetting” into freedom from commitment or absolute independence.*
